# Key Concepts from "Building Effective AI Agents"

**Workflows vs. Agents:**
"Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths" while "agents are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage."

**Routing to Specialized Prompts/Tools:**
"Routing works well for complex tasks where there are distinct categories that are better handled separately," allowing teams to build specialized prompts and prevent optimization for one input type from harming performance on others.

**Poka-Yoke Tool Design:**
The guidance suggests you should "Change the arguments so that it is harder to make mistakes." The document illustrates this through their SWE-bench work, where requiring absolute filepaths prevented model errors with relative paths.

**Guardrails/Checks in Code:**
"You can add programmatic checks (see 'gate' in the diagram below) on any intermediate steps to ensure that the process is still on track" within prompt chaining workflows.

**Sandboxing:**
"We recommend extensive testing in sandboxed environments, along with the appropriate guardrails" before deploying autonomous agents due to their higher costs and potential for compounding errors.

**Keeping Agents Simple:**
The core principle emphasizes maintaining "simplicity in your agent's design" and notes that "agent implementation is often straightforward—just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop."

The documentation describes three core modes controlled via `tool_choice` in `generation_config`:

- **`none`**: The model cannot make function calls
- **`validated`**: The model ensures adherence to the function schema

The documentation covers implementation patterns like:
- Defining clear function descriptions and parameters
- Supporting parallel function calls for independent operations
- Chaining multiple function calls for complex workflows (compositional function calling)
- Using stateless mode by managing conversation history client-side

However, the content provided **does not include detailed guidance** on tool validation strategies, error handling approaches, or explicit best practices for tool selection optimization.

The focus is primarily on technical implementation rather than strategic guidance for managing large tool sets.

content.content:
---
title: Tool use with prompt caching
url: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-use-with-prompt-caching
description: Cache tool definitions across turns and understand what invalidates your cache.
---

This page covers prompt caching for tool definitions: where to place `cache_control` breakpoints, how `defer_loading` preserves your cache, and what invalidates it. For general prompt caching, see [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching).

## cache\_control on tool definitions

Place `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` on the last tool in your `tools` array. This caches the entire tool-definitions prefix, from the first tool through the marked breakpoint:

```json
{
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "get_weather",
      "description": "Get the current weather in a given location",
      "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "location": { "type": "string" }
        },
        "required": ["location"]
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "get_time",
      "description": "Get the current time in a given time zone",
      "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "timezone": { "type": "string" }
        },
        "required": ["timezone"]
      },
      "cache_control": { "type": "ephemeral" }
    }
  ]
}
```

For `mcp_toolset`, the `cache_control` breakpoint lands on the last tool in the set. You don't control tool order within an MCP toolset, so place the breakpoint on the `mcp_toolset` entry itself and the API applies it to the final expanded tool.

The [computer use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool) and [browser use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/browser-use-tool) toolset entries follow the same rule: place `cache_control` on the toolset entry itself, and the breakpoint lands after the toolset's definition. It isn't accepted inside a member's `configs` entry, because the toolset's members load as one definition. Within a [batch action](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool#batch-actions), a `cache_control` marker on any of the turn's member `tool_use` or `tool_result` blocks is accepted and takes effect at the end of that batch, so several markers in one batch act as a single breakpoint. Each marker still counts toward the request's limit of [four breakpoints](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching#when-to-use-multiple-breakpoints), so use one per turn.

## defer\_loading and cache preservation

Deferred tools are not included in the system-prompt prefix. When the model discovers a deferred tool through [tool search](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool), the definition is appended inline as a `tool_reference` block in the conversation history. The prefix is untouched, so prompt caching is preserved.

This means adding tools dynamically through tool search does not break your cache. You can start a conversation with a small set of always-loaded tools (cached), let the model discover additional tools as needed, and keep the same cache hit across every turn.

## cache\_control on tool definitions

Place `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` on the last tool in your `tools` array. This caches the entire tool-definitions prefix, from the first tool through the marked breakpoint:

```json
    {
      "name": "get_weather",
      "description": "Get the current weather in a given location",
      "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "location": { "type": "string" }
        },
        "required": ["location"]
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "get_time",
      "description": "Get the current time in a given time zone",
      "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "timezone": { "type": "string" }
        },
        "required": ["timezone"]
      },
      "cache_control": { "type": "ephemeral" }
    }
  ]
}
```

# Tool Set Guidance from Anthropic

According to the article, Anthropic recommends curating a **"minimal viable set of tools"** for agents to improve reliability and context management.

The document warns against **"bloated tool sets that cover too much functionality"** which create inefficiency problems.

Regarding decision-making, it states: **"If a human engineer can't definitively say which tool should be used in a given situation, an AI agent can't be expected to do better."**

On functionality overlap, the article advises building tools with **"minimal overlap in functionality,"** comparing well-designed tool sets to organized codebases that are self-contained and robust.

The core principle is that limiting tools prevents confusion, maintains focus, and keeps context lean during agent operations.

Based on the search results, I found information about the `function_calling_config` and `allowed_function_names` parameter in the Gemini API.

The `allowed_function_names` parameter is used within `function_calling_config` to specify which functions the model is allowed to call. In the example shown, it's configured with `mode: 'ANY'` and `allowed_function_names: ['get_product_sku']`, restricting the model to only call the `get_product_sku` function even though multiple functions are declared.

This configuration allows you to control which of your declared functions the model can actually invoke during a request. It's useful for:

1. **Restricting function access** - Limiting which functions can be called in a particular request
2. **Security** - Preventing the model from calling sensitive functions
3. **Flow control** - Guiding the model toward specific functions for a given task

The configuration is part of the `toolConfig` object that you pass to the Gemini API when making requests with function declarations.

content.text:
My recommendation matches what the major providers publish. The check turned up one catch that the plan has to handle, and two refinements.

## Each point against the providers' guidance

| Recommendation | What the providers say | Consistent? |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Offer each chat only the tools its state allows** (adding: find/add; after adding: also connect; change/connect chats: no add tools) | **Anthropic:** give agents a "minimal viable set of tools" with "minimal overlap". If a human engineer "can't definitively say which tool should be used", neither can the agent. **OpenAI Agents SDK:** tools can be enabled or disabled "based on context, user preferences, or runtime conditions". **Google Gemini:** `allowed_function_names` restricts which declared functions can be called. | Yes |
| **2. The app refuses out-of-place calls itself, with a clear error** | **OpenAI Agents SDK:** hiding a tool "does not replace authorization… Enforce those checks inside the tool implementation." **Anthropic:** write error responses that "clearly communicate specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes." | Yes |
| **3. Fill in the printer from the chat, not from the model** | **OpenAI:** "Don't make the model fill arguments you already know." **Anthropic:** "poka-yoke" tools, i.e. change the arguments "so that it is harder to make mistakes." | Yes |
| **4. Keep the full tool list, restrict with `tool_choice.allowed_tools`** | **OpenAI:** `allowed_tools` exists so you can restrict tools and "not modify the list of tools you pass in, so you can maximize savings from prompt caching". Its caching guide says to keep definitions stable and restrict with `allowed_tools`. | Yes, for OpenAI, which the app uses |
| **5. Test it with evals from real use** | **Anthropic:** "Start by generating lots of evaluation tasks, grounded in real world uses." | Yes |

The reason for the change also lines up with them. OpenAI's soft limit is "fewer than 20 functions" per turn, and we have 8. So the point isn't reducing the count; it's removing tools that are invalid in the current state, which is exactly the kind of overlap Anthropic warns about.

## The catch I found by testing

I sent two tools, `ping` and `pong`, allowed only `pong`, and asked the model to "call the ping tool". On both OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini and DeepSeek through OpenRouter, the restriction held 3 of 3 times. But every time the model **called `pong` instead of saying it couldn't call `ping`**.

Hiding a tool can therefore push the model to the nearest allowed tool instead of an honest answer. In a change chat, "also add my Prusa" might turn into a `printer_change` call or an attempt to connect, instead of "start a new add chat from Home". So the plan needs:
- a line telling the model what to say when someone asks for something the chat can't do. This fits the prompt's existing scope rule for change and connect chats.
- the planned test case for "add a different printer" in a change chat, checking that the model explains instead of calling some other tool. This case matters more than I'd assumed.

## Two refinements
- **Anthropic's API has no `allowed_tools` equivalent.** Its only options are changing the tool list, which invalidates the whole prompt cache, or setting `tool_choice`, which invalidates only the conversation part. The app only talks to OpenAI today, and each printer chat starts with an empty cache anyway, so this costs nothing now. It's worth one line in the guide in case the provider changes.
- **OpenRouter supports `allowed_tools`, though its docs don't mention it.** The test above shows the restriction held on the pinned DeepSeek hosts. The prompt test script can therefore use the same restriction as the app.

A related point that isn't part of the recommendation: OpenAI recommends strict mode on every tool and structuring parameters so invalid calls can't happen. Three of the eight printer tools aren't strict, because they have optional fields, and `printer_connect` lets the model send contradictory fields (a device ID plus an address). The app's registry refuses those calls, so it's safe as is. Tightening them would be a separate cleanup.

**Verdict:** the recommendation holds, with one addition to the plan: tell the model how to answer requests the chat can't handle, and test that. Want me to implement it?

Sources:
- [OpenAI: Function calling guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling)
- [OpenAI: Prompt caching guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- [OpenAI Agents SDK: Tools](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tools/)
- [Anthropic: Writing effective tools for agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)
- [Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
- [Anthropic: Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Anthropic: Tool use with prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-use-with-prompt-caching)
- [Google: Function calling with the Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/function-calling)
- [OpenRouter: Responses API tool calling](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/reference/responses/tool-calling)

content.text:
No, it isn't universal, so the plan shouldn't depend on it. There's a version that works on every API and costs no extra cache misses.

## Which APIs can restrict tools without changing the list

| API | Can restrict which tools are callable while keeping the same list? |
|---|---|
| OpenAI (Responses and Chat Completions) | Yes: `tool_choice: {type: "allowed_tools", …}` |
| Google Gemini | Yes: `function_calling_config.allowed_function_names` |
| Anthropic | **No.** `tool_choice` accepts only auto, any, one named tool, or none. Some newer models reject even "any" and "one named tool". |
| OpenRouter | Passed through in my DeepSeek test, but not documented, and it depends on the host serving the model |
| Self-hosted open models (vLLM, Ollama and similar) | **No.** Generally auto, required, none or one named tool |

So `allowed_tools` is out.

## The universal version
Only two things are needed, and every tool-calling API supports both:

1. **Choose the tool list once, when the chat opens, from its mode, and don't change it during the chat.** Every API supports sending a different tool list per conversation.
   - **Add chat:** all eight tools, as today. It really can need every one: find and add, correct the nozzle, then connect and finish.
   - **Change and Connect chats:** five tools (change, connection status, connect, printer settings, finish), without `printer_identify`, `printer_add` and `printer_manual_setup`.
2. **The app refuses any call that's invalid for the chat's current state,** with a clear error. For example: connecting before anything has been added (the app already refuses this), adding in a change chat, or changing a printer other than the chat's own. This is plain code in the app, so it works the same on every provider.

What this drops from my earlier plan: growing the Add chat's tools after a printer is added. The app's refusal covers that state instead. The model-side finding still applies: with an add tool unavailable, a model may reach for the nearest allowed tool. So the prompt should say what to answer when asked for something the chat can't do, and the planned test for "add a different printer" in a change chat stays.

## Will it invalidate cached prompts?
Every provider caches by exact prefix, and the tool list is part of the prefix, so any change to it breaks the cache from that point on. What matters is when the list changes:

- **During a chat: never,** because the list is fixed for the whole chat. Every request after the first reuses the cache, as today.
- **Between chats: nothing is lost.** Caches are shared across chats that have the same prefix; that's how Add chats get most of their roughly 28 KB prompt cached. Each mode would still always send the same tool list, so every Add chat shares one cached prefix and every Change chat another. Add and Change never shared a cache anyway, since their instructions already differ.
- **Add chats aren't affected at all:** their tool list stays exactly as it is.
- **The only extra miss is once, at rollout,** for the first Change or Connect request after the update, because its prefix is new. Those prompts are small; the guide measured the change prompt below the size OpenAI caches at all.

The only design that would have cost cache misses is changing the tool list mid-chat, and this version doesn't. That makes it the right choice even setting provider support aside.

content.text:
You're right to catch that. I used "state" for two different things and blurred them. I earlier proposed that the list follow the state, and then changed the plan without saying so clearly. The final design separates them:

- **The tool list depends on the chat's *mode*: Add, Change or Connect.** The mode is set when the chat opens and never changes during it (I checked `PrinterConversation`: nothing changes the mode mid-chat). So the list really is fixed per chat.
- **Whether a particular call is allowed depends on the chat's *state*,** which does change mid-chat: whether a printer has been added yet, whether a connection is in progress, which printer the chat is about. The app checks that when a call arrives and refuses the call with a clear error. It never changes the list.

So the chat does have states. They're just enforced by the app's refusals instead of by what the model is shown.

An example with an Add chat:

| Point in the chat | Tools listed | A `printer_connect` call |
|---|---|---|
| Before anything is added | all 8 | Refused: "add the printer first". The app already does this today. |
| After a printer is added | the same 8 | Allowed |

The cost is that early in an Add chat the model sees tools it can't use yet. That's acceptable: the prompt already says to connect only after adding, and a refusal tells it what to do if it tries early. The alternative, growing the list after the add, would give up the prompt cache once in every Add chat, and that's the big prompt.

input.description: Read the guide's tool-loading principles

content.content:
## Tool budget and tool shape

Tool count is bounded by what a turn loads, not by what the app can do. The evidence behind these rules: OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest; Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools targeting high-impact workflows and names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error; a [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured a generic thin-tool interface below raw SQL and domain-shaped tools far above both; and the "god tool" that dispatches many unrelated actions through one `action` parameter is a documented anti-pattern. The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, two thirds of it output schema.

- **Loading, for now.** Every registered tool loads on every turn in both adapters: the in-app adapter sends the full function list with each request, and MCP `tools/list` returns the whole catalog. This is the simplest correct behaviour and it keeps the tools array byte-identical across a chat, which is what OpenAI's prompt cache keys on. The budget of 20 definitions per turn is a measured trigger, not a gate: the live regression records definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens per request, and the journey catalog below will exceed 20 definitions from its first milestone. That is accepted until those measurements show selection errors or context pressure.
- **The baseline, measured on Windows against the live app.** After M5: in-app 25 definitions and 29,148 bytes, MCP 26 and 33,013 over two `tools/list` pages. After M4: in-app 20 definitions and 21,594 bytes, MCP 21 and 24,923 (24,901 through the offline helper recipe). After M3: in-app 20 definitions and 19,331 bytes, MCP 21 and 22,661 (22,639 through the offline helper recipe). After M2: in-app 18 definitions and 12,721 bytes, MCP 16 and 13,911 (13,894 through the offline helper recipe). After M1: in-app 11 definitions and 6,482 bytes, MCP 9 and 6,915. At M0 it was in-app 7 and 3,145 bytes, MCP 5 and 3,147.

  The `--live-agent` regression at both points says what that costs. The first request of a conversation caches nothing and pays for the whole catalog: 803 tokens at M0, 1,733 at M1, so four more definitions cost about 930 tokens, once. Every later request in the same conversation came back 77 to 92 per cent cached (5,864 in, 5,376 cached at M1), because the tools array is byte-identical across a chat and that is what the cache keys on. At M2 the same regression's eleven requests took 2,875 to 6,763 input tokens with 42 to 91 per cent cached; none started cold, because an earlier run of the same day had warmed the cache for the shared prefix, so the M2 cold cost is not measured by that run.

  So the cost of a definition is what it adds to the *first* request of each conversation, not to every turn, and the budget stays a trigger rather than a gate. What would change that reading: a catalog large enough to make the first request of every conversation expensive on its own, or transcripts showing the model choosing the wrong tool. Watch both; neither has appeared yet.
- **The printer panel's session is the exception to "every tool loads".** Home's printer panel runs its own conversation with exactly one tool per mode: `printer_identify` when adding a printer, `printer_change` when changing one (`PrinterConversation::session_tools`). The app decides the tools; the words are the page's (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` for the instructions, `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` for the notes the model reads after a tap), and a turn the page has not yet written them for is refused rather than sent with the project assistant's prompt. A Change session that could also identify a printer could clear the card of the printer it is about. Measured 2026-09-18 on the app's own request bodies against `gpt-5.4-mini`: Add sends one definition of 597 bytes and instructions of 28,425 bytes (the rules plus the 383-line printer list), about 11,540 input tokens per request, of which 11,008 came back cached on every request after the first of the day; the cold first request cached nothing. Change sends one definition of 832 bytes and about 552 input tokens, below the size OpenAI caches at all. Neither session carries the project: no workspace in the turn, none in a tool result.
- **Deferral, when the measurements say so.** Use the platform's own deferral, never a hand-rolled switcher. On the in-app side that is OpenAI's `tool_search` with `defer_loading: true` on the Responses API, documented for `gpt-5.4` and later; support on the pinned `gpt-5.4-mini` is unverified. On the MCP side clients defer on their own, as Claude Code does. Toolsets are the deferral unit, and OpenAI recommends fewer than ten functions per namespace. An enable-toolset tool that rewrites the tools array breaks the prompt cache on every switch and is not to be built.

content.text:
You're right, and that one's on me. I made it sound more complicated than it is. Neither "mode" nor "state" is new: both already exist in the code, and I shouldn't have used them as design vocabulary.

- The **mode** is just which chat was opened: add, change or connect. The code has always had it.
- The **state** is just what the chat already remembers: which printer it's about, and whether something was added. The app already uses it: it refuses a connect before anything has been added.

## Is "all eight tools" consistent with the guide?
The guide says two different things, and the code matches one and breaks the other:

1. **The general rule** (tool budget section): "Every registered tool loads on every turn." It keeps the tool list identical across a chat for caching, and it names the evidence that would change that: "transcripts showing the model choosing the wrong tool". It also bans rewriting the tool list mid-chat. **All eight everywhere is consistent with this.**
2. **The printer-panel exception:** "exactly one tool per mode". **All eight contradicts this.**

## Which is more correct?
- **Against the one-tool-per-mode exception, the code is right.** The exception's only reason (not wiping the printer card) disappeared when the card was removed. And one tool per step caused a real failure: after adding a printer, there was no tool to connect it. The exception is out of date and should be deleted.
- **Against the general rule, the code is also consistent.** The only question is whether the rule's trigger ("the model choosing the wrong tool") has been met. The evidence is thin: a few test-script runs where a model called `printer_add` or `printer_identify` in a change chat. One of those was the app's own model, and the app refused that call because the printer id was invalid. There are no reports from real use.

## What that means for my recommendation
Given the guide's own rule, I'm walking back part of what I proposed. The simplest correct version is:

1. **Keep all eight tools in every chat,** as the code and the guide's general rule already do.
2. **Add the app's refusals.** They're needed whatever the tool list is, because hiding a tool doesn't stop a bad call. Refuse adding in a change or connect chat, and refuse changing a printer other than the chat's own, with a clear error, the same way the app already refuses connecting before adding.
3. **Measure before doing more.** The test script now has the "add a different printer from a change chat" case. Only if it shows the model attempting wrong tools often, and not recovering after the refusal, would removing tools from change and connect chats be worth doing. The guide's rule asks for exactly that kind of evidence.
4. **Fix the guide:** delete the stale exception, and describe the refusals.

That's one concept (the app refuses calls that make no sense), no change to the tool list, and nothing that touches caching.

# CLAUDE.md - Testing Guide for OrcaSlicer

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for Claude Code when writing, maintaining, and understanding tests in the OrcaSlicer codebase.

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RULES - MUST FOLLOW

### 1. **SECTIONS IN LOOPS - NEVER REUSE NAMES**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause unpredictable behavior
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Bad loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        SECTION("Same name") {  // WRONG! Same name used multiple times
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use DYNAMIC_SECTION or incorporate counter
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Good loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        DYNAMIC_SECTION("Section " << i) {  // Unique name per iteration
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

### 2. **THREAD SAFETY - ASSERTIONS ARE NOT THREAD-SAFE**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([]() {
            REQUIRE(some_calculation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
        });
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Synchronize results, test on main thread
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    std::atomic<int> passed{0};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([&passed]() {
            if (some_calculation() == expected) {
                passed++;
            }
        });
    }
    
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    REQUIRE(passed == 4);  // Test results on main thread
}
```

### 3. **EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION - AVOID BINARY OPERATORS**
❌ **WRONG**: Cannot decompose properly
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0 && b < 10);  // Shows "false" on failure, not individual values
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Split into separate assertions
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0);
REQUIRE(b < 10);  // Each shows individual values on failure
```

### 4. **FLOATING POINT - NEVER USE APPROX**
❌ **WRONG**: Approx is deprecated and asymmetric
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_value == Catch::Approx(expected));  // Deprecated!
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use floating point matchers
```cpp
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));     // 4 ULPs apart
```

### 5. **TEST ORDERING - ALWAYS USE RANDOM ORDER**
✅ **REQUIRED**: For CI/CD and development
```bash
# Essential flags for running tests
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# For test sharding (parallel execution), share random seed
./tests --order rand --shard-index 0 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
```

## Overview of OrcaSlicer's Testing Framework

OrcaSlicer uses **Catch2 v3** (currently v3.11.0, vendored in `tests/catch2/`) as its primary testing framework. The test suite is organized into several modules that mirror the project's architectural components:

> **Note**: Test files include the framework via `#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>` (the v3 single-header convenience include). All v3 features described in this guide are available.

### Test Structure
```
tests/
├── CMakeLists.txt              # Main test configuration
├── catch_main.hpp              # Custom test reporter
├── libslic3r/                  # Core library tests (21 test files)
├── fff_print/                  # FFF printing tests (12 test files)
├── sla_print/                  # SLA printing tests (4 test files)
├── libnest2d/                  # 2D nesting tests
├── slic3rutils/               # Utility tests
├── data/                      # Test data files and meshes
└── catch2/                    # Catch2 framework files
```

### Build Integration
- Tests are built using CMake with `catch_discover_tests()` integration
- Each test module creates a separate executable (e.g., `libslic3r_tests`, `fff_print_tests`)
- Test data directory is available via `TEST_DATA_DIR` preprocessor definition
- Custom verbose console reporter provides detailed test output

## Catch2 Features Guide

### Basic Assertions
```cpp
// Primary assertions - stop test on failure
REQUIRE(expression);
REQUIRE_FALSE(expression);

// Continuing assertions - continue test after failure  
CHECK(expression);
CHECK_FALSE(expression);

// Non-failing checks - record result but don't fail test
CHECK_NOFAIL(expression);  // Useful for assumptions that might be violated
```

### Exception Testing
```cpp
// Verify no exception is thrown
REQUIRE_NOTHROW(function_call());

// Verify any exception is thrown
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());

// Verify specific exception type
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(function_call(), SpecificException);

// Verify exception message
REQUIRE_THROWS_WITH(function_call(), "Expected error message");

// Verify exception with matchers (for partial matching)

                       Catch::Matchers::Message("contains this"));
```

### Complex Assertions with Matchers
```cpp
#include <catch2/matchers/catch_matchers.hpp>

// String matchers
using Catch::Matchers::StartsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::EndsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::ContainsSubstring;
using Catch::Matchers::Equals;
using Catch::Matchers::Matches;  // Regex matching

REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, StartsWith("Expected prefix"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, ContainsSubstring("middle part"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, Matches(".*pattern.*"));

using Catch::Matchers::WithinRel;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinULP;

REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));     // Absolute tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));      // Relative tolerance (1%)
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));         // ULP difference (requires IEEE-754)

// Combining matchers
```


## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)

Use RAII and smart pointers in tests:

- **It depends on a thread or a lifetime the page does not have.**

The printer panel is the example. The app sends the page facts only: sizes, spools, which printer is on a card, what a change changed. The page writes every word from them. It writes the model's instructions (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`) and hands them over with `printer_instructions`. It writes the panel's own words, the opening line and the note that goes with each tap (`AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts`). The opening goes over with `printer_opening`, and a tap's note travels in the tap's payload.

The app decides which one tool each mode offers, checks every call, and refuses a turn that has no instructions rather than falling back to the project assistant's prompt. It posts the opening once per session, and a tap's note only when the tap goes through, bounded to 2 KB. It still writes the notes for what only it can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, its model id is not on the list, or a save or undo failed.

lines=s.split('\n')
def find(prefix):
    idx=[i for i,l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith(prefix)]
    assert len(idx)==1,(prefix,idx); return idx[0]
# 1. the panel bullet
i=find("- **The printer panel's session is the exception to \"every tool loads\".**")
lines[i]=("- **The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set.** Home's printer panel runs its own conversation "
 "(`PrinterConversation`), offered the eight printer tools and no others, the same list in every mode, so the list stays "
 "byte-identical across a conversation and across conversations of the same mode. What a call may do depends on the "
 "conversation, and `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses the rest before any card, with an error that says where "
 "to go instead: finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`, `printer_manual_setup`) only in an Add "
 "conversation, since a Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has and an add there would "
 "save another printer and move the conversation onto it; `printer_change` only on the printer the conversation is about, "
 "once there is one; the connection tools only once there is a saved printer. A list that differs by mode is not used: "
 "the conversation's own refusal is needed whatever the model is shown, and a restricted-but-stable list "
 "(`tool_choice` with `allowed_tools`) exists only on some providers. What would change that: transcripts of the model "
 "reaching for a refused tool and not recovering, which `tests/printer_prompt` measures (`change-add-another`). Until "
 "2026-09-23 the panel offered one tool per mode (7f66e75b07), to keep a lookup from clearing the pinned card of the "
 "printer a Change session was about; that card is gone (4d4f9e466b), and one tool per step left an Add conversation "
 "with no tool to connect the printer it had just added (8334b3395b). The app decides the tools; the words are the "
 "page's (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` for the instructions, `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` for the notes the "
 "model reads after a tap), and a turn the page has not yet written them for is refused rather than sent with the "
 "project assistant's prompt. The Add instructions carry the whole printer list, about 28 KB, which caches as a fixed "
 "prefix. No printer conversation carries the project: no workspace in the turn, none in a tool result.")
# 2. adapter note
i=find("- the printer panel's two tools carry only the `Printer` exposure")
lines[i]=("- the printer panel's eight tools carry only the `Printer` exposure: neither adapter lists them, and the panel's "
 "conversation offers all of them in every mode and refuses what does not fit it (see \"Tool budget and tool shape\"). "
 "They take no `planId` (`joins_plans` excludes them), and what the model reads back from them is the tool's own result, "
 "not the host's workspace envelope.")
# 3. table rows
i=find("| `printer_change` |")
j=find("| `printer_identify` |")
assert j==i+1
panel="printer panel, every mode"
rows={
"printer_add":"| `printer_add` | Save the printer the person confirmed, so they can prepare prints for it | mutation, on the person's yes in the conversation | "+panel+"; refused outside an Add conversation | one catalog id and an optional nozzle it ships | `OrcaPrinterBackend::add_printer` (a named printer from the model's profile) | the printer as saved; `not_in_this_conversation`, `unknown_printer`, `unknown_nozzle`, `already_added`, `add_failed` |",
"printer_change":"| `printer_change` | Change a printer the person owns: the nozzle size now on it. What is loaded is the printer's to report, not a thing to save | mutation, on the person's yes in the conversation | "+panel+" | only the printer the conversation is about, once there is one; never the open project | `Printers::change_named_printer_nozzle` (writes the profile without selecting it) | what changed, before and after, and the printer as it now is; `no_printer`, `other_printer`, `unknown_printer`, `nothing_to_change`, `unknown_nozzle`, `change_failed` |",
"printer_connect":"| `printer_connect` | Connect the printer the conversation is about | mutation; a card where the person types the access code or API key | "+panel+" | a Bambu Lab `deviceId` from the status, or a Moonraker or OctoPrint address the person gave | `OrcaPrinterBackend::connect_printer`, `connect_host` | `connecting`, `verified` or `failed` with a message; the outcome of a wait arrives as a note; `no_printer`, `connection_unavailable`, `unknown_device`, `address_needed` |",
"printer_connection_status":"| `printer_connection_status` | Know whether the printer can be reached, and which Bambu Lab printers are in LAN mode | read-only | "+panel+" | the printer the conversation is about | `OrcaPrinterBackend::connection`, `prepare_connection` | provider, state, message, saved address and host type, LAN-mode candidates; `no_printer` |",
"printer_identify":"| `printer_identify` | Show the printers the model decided the person means | read-only | "+panel+"; refused outside an Add conversation | 1 to 3 ids copied from the printer list in the instructions | `PrinterCatalog::panel_printers` | each printer's brand, model, build volume, nozzle sizes and what adding it assumes (nozzle; plate and filament, `null` where the profile names none); `not_in_this_conversation`, `too_many`, `unknown_printer`, `unknown_nozzle` |",
"printer_manual_connection":"| `printer_manual_connection` | Open the printer's settings, where the person enters connection details or anything else themselves | mutation (opens a window) | "+panel+" | the printer the conversation is about | `Printers::open_named_printer_settings` | `opened`; `no_printer` |",
"printer_manual_setup":"| `printer_manual_setup` | Browse OrcaSlicer's full printer list | mutation (the person may add printers there) | "+panel+"; refused outside an Add conversation | none | `OrcaPrinterBackend::run_manual_setup` | whether anything was applied and the printers added; `not_in_this_conversation` |",
"printer_setup_finish":"| `printer_setup_finish` | Close the printer conversation when the person says they are done | mutation | "+panel+" | the panel | `IConversationHost::close_panel` | `closed` |",
}
del lines[i:j+1]
table=[k for k,l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("| `")]
names={k:lines[k].split('`')[1] for k in table}
for name in sorted(rows, reverse=True):
    # insert before the first row whose name sorts after it, within the tool table (starting row after header at 337)
    cands=[k for k in table if k>300 and k<500 and names[k]>name]
    pos=min(cands)
    lines.insert(pos,rows[name])
    table=[k for k,l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("| `")]; names={k:lines[k].split('`')[1] for k in table}
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write('\n'.join(lines))
EOF
grep -n "^| \`printer_\|^| \`presets_list\|^| \`project" agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md | cut -c1-60

toolUseResult.newString: The app decides the tools -- the eight printer tools, the same in every mode -- checks every call, refuses one that does not fit the conversation (adding a printer outside an Add conversation, changing a printer other than the one it is about), and refuses a turn that has no instructions rather than falling back to the project assistant's prompt.

lines: The printer panel is the example. The app sends the page facts only: sizes, spools, which printer is on a card, what a change changed. The page writes every word from them. It writes the model's instructions (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`) and hands them over with `printer_instructions`. It writes the panel's own words, the opening line and the note that goes with each tap (`AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts`). The opening goes over with `printer_opening`, and a tap's note travels in the tap's payload.

-The app decides which one tool each mode offers, checks every call, and refuses a turn that has no instructions rather than falling back to the project assistant's prompt. It posts the opening once per session, and a tap's note only when the tap goes through, bounded to 2 KB. It still writes the notes for what only it can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, its model id is not on the list, or a save or undo failed.

+The app decides the tools -- the eight printer tools, the same in every mode -- checks every call, refuses one that does not fit the conversation (adding a printer outside an Add conversation, changing a printer other than the one it is about), and refuses a turn that has no instructions rather than falling back to the project assistant's prompt. It posts the opening once per session, and a tap's note only when the tap goes through, bounded to 2 KB. It still writes the notes for what only it can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, its model id is not on the list, or a save or undo failed.

Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. Local resource packaging must work on all three. The demonstrated prototype used a single-file local bundle to avoid WKWebView `file:` subresource failures; production keeps that approach, and CMake now produces the bundle from the TypeScript/React sources.

cd /c/src/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/printer-conversation-panel-af11cb; git add -A agent-docs/jusprin src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin tests/agent tests/printer_prompt; git status --short; cat > /tmp/msg3.txt <<'EOF'
Refuse printer tool calls that do not fit the conversation

Every printer conversation is offered all eight printer tools, so the tool
list stays the same for the prompt cache, but nothing checked that a call
fit the conversation. printer_add in a Change conversation saved a second
printer and moved the conversation onto it, and printer_change took any
saved printer's name, even in an Add conversation before anything was
added. Test runs showed models calling printer_add and printer_identify in
Change conversations.

PrinterConversation::preflight_tool, which runs before any card, now
refuses, with an error that says where to go instead:
- printer_identify, printer_add and printer_manual_setup outside an Add
  conversation (not_in_this_conversation: another printer is added with
  + Add printer on Home);
- printer_change before the conversation has a printer (no_printer), and on
  a printer other than the one it is about (other_printer, or
  unknown_printer for a name that is not saved).
change() no longer repeats the name check.

The tool list is not scoped per mode. Hiding a tool does not stop a call,
so the refusal is needed either way, and a restricted-but-stable list
(tool_choice allowed_tools) exists only on some providers. The docs said
otherwise: mcp-tool-extension-guide.md still described one tool per mode,
a design reversed on 2026-09-23 (8334b3395b) whose reason, the pinned
printer card, was removed on 2026-09-22. It and architecture.md now describe
the eight tools and the refusals, and the guide's tool table lists all eight.

tests/printer_prompt answers the tools with the same refusals and adds
change-add-another ("I also have a Prusa MK4S, can you add it too?"): nothing
is ever added; the reply said where to add it in 15 of 20 runs on DeepSeek
V4 Flash and 9 to 15 of 20 with --app, often "Yes, I can add it" with no
tool called at all. The next commit addresses that in the prompt.

Verified: agent_bridge_tests 265 cases pass, with new cases for each
refusal and a host test that the refusal reaches the model; AgentUI 213
pass; shell_harness --printer-live 0 failures.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 timeout 90 git commit -F /tmp/msg3.txt < /dev/null 2>&1 | tail -2; echo "exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

**`829dfeb8c1`: the app refuses printer tool calls that don't fit the chat.** Every printer chat still gets all eight tools, so nothing changes for caching or across providers. But before any call runs, the app now checks it:
- **In a change or connect chat,** finding or adding a printer is refused, with a message telling the model that another printer is added with "+ Add printer" on Home. Before this, an add in a change chat really saved a second printer and switched the chat to it.
- **Changing a printer** is refused before the chat has a printer, and for any printer other than the one the chat is about. Before this, it accepted any saved printer's name.
- **The guide and `architecture.md`** now describe this. The stale "one tool per mode" text is gone, with a note on why it changed and when to reconsider, and the guide's tool table now lists all eight printer tools; it had only two.

The app's model often replied "Yes, I can add it" without calling any tool, so nothing reached the app to refuse. The change and connect instructions now say another printer isn't added here and point to "+ Add printer" on Home. The add chat's instructions are unchanged.

content.text:
No. It isn't better; it scored in the same range as DeepSeek, and at 3 runs per case the gaps between them are mostly noise. I kept bringing it in for one reason: it's the model the app actually sends users' chats to today (the app's default is `gpt-5.4-mini`). So a prompt that works on DeepSeek but not on it would still be broken for real users.

But I overdid it. You decided DeepSeek on the pinned hosts is the model for judging prompts, and I then ran and reported both models on every change anyway. That doubled the test cost, doubled the numbers you had to read, and made the app's model look like a second judge it was never meant to be. It also matters less going forward: you'll support other providers soon, so today's default model won't necessarily be what users get.

From here, I'll judge and report prompt changes on DeepSeek only. The README currently says to run `--app` once before a prompt change ships. I can keep that as a single final check, or drop the line so DeepSeek is the only reference. Which do you prefer?

# Printer panel prompt tests

The printer panel's assistant is a system prompt
(`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`), eight printer
tools, and the chat. `run_prompt_tests.py` sends the live model the same
requests the app sends. It answers the tools the way the app answers them for
a fixed printer, then checks what the model did. The app does not run.

```bash
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... OPENAI_API_KEY=... tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py
```

Prompts are judged on DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, served only by the
hosts that answer the app's notes (decided 2026-09-28; see "Which model").
`OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is for that model, `OPENAI_API_KEY` for the judge.

A run is one sample of a model that answers differently each time, so each case
runs several times, in parallel, and reports a count. By default one invocation
runs at most 100 conversations (`RUN_BUDGET`), shared by the cases it runs: 3
each for the 28 cases, and at most 20 for a case run alone. `--runs N` sets
the count per case instead; use it to look closer at one case. By default
every run must pass; `--must-pass N` lowers the bar. `--verbose` prints every
conversation, not only the failed ones.

## Judging a prompt change

Run the cases before and after the edit and compare the counts; "Baseline"
below has the counts to start from. The script renders the prompt from the
TypeScript source on every run, so nothing needs building. At the default
three runs a case catches a behaviour that fails often, not one that fails one
time in twenty; when a case fails, or to judge the edit it was written for,
run that case alone, where it gets 20 runs.
Differences of a few runs out of 20 are noise; look for a clear gap.

Run the prompt before the edit with `--prompt-rev HEAD` (any git revision
works): the page's source is read as it was there, and the checkout is left
alone. Run both at the same time, so both meet the same hosts and the same
day. A baseline recorded earlier is a guide, not a control: the same prompt
scored 76, 76 and 74 of 84 on the default model in three runs, and 80 and 78
with `--app`, so compare against a before run made alongside the after run.
Paired this way, a real effect shows plainly: on 2026-09-28 a two-line edit
took `add-not-now-done` from 19 to 3 of 20 while its own case improved.

Run every case, not only the one the edit is for. The three sessions share one
prompt, so a line written for one of them reaches the other two; a fix is one
whose own case improves while no other case drops.

Before a prompt change ships, run it once more with `--app`: the app's own
model, gpt-5.4-mini on OpenAI. The two models fail in different places, and
people talk to the app's.

Every reply in every case is also held to the rules the prompt sets for all
replies: a `Choices:` line the page draws as intended (on the last line, two
to four choices under 30 characters, or Done alone; read as
`replyChoices.ts` reads it), and none of the internal words the prompt rules
out (profile, preset, catalog, a tool's name). A reply that breaks one fails
its run, whatever the case checks.

A few checks are about what a reply says, which no string test can read.
Those ask a stronger model (`JUDGE_MODEL`, pinned) one narrow yes-or-no
question about the conversation's last reply, and the run prints its reason.
Read the reasons of the runs that fail before trusting a count: a question
worded too broadly fails good replies.

## What keeps it faithful to the app

- **The system prompt and the opening line** come from the page's own source,
  through `render_prompt.mjs` and the page's esbuild. This needs node and the
  AgentUI npm install.
- **`printer_tools.json`** is the tool list the app sends in the printer panel.
  `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` fails when it drifts from the registry.
  Regenerate it with
  `JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PRINTER_TOOLS=1 agent_bridge_tests '[printer]'`.
- **The chat history** is built the way `AgentHost` and `OpenAIResponsesAgent`
  build it: each earlier assistant message's words, then the tool calls it
  made with their results (replayed since `jusprin-newui` 115e2776bf); then
  this turn's message, tool calls and results. A call the app refused before
  it ran is not replayed, because the app never recorded it.
- **Tool answers** are what the app returned for the in-process fake Bambu
  printer, recorded from a real run.

The app streams its requests and this script does not. By default a different
model answers them (see "Which model"); `--app` sends them to the app's own.

## Cases

- `connect-bambu`: connect a saved Bambu Lab A1 mini that is on the network.
  Passes when the model opens `printer_connect`'s card for it. Before the app
  replayed earlier tool results, it failed about a third of the time: the model
  looked up the printer's id in one turn, and on "connect it" in the next it had

# CLAUDE.md - Testing Guide for OrcaSlicer

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for Claude Code when writing, maintaining, and understanding tests in the OrcaSlicer codebase.

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RULES - MUST FOLLOW

### 1. **SECTIONS IN LOOPS - NEVER REUSE NAMES**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause unpredictable behavior
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Bad loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        SECTION("Same name") {  // WRONG! Same name used multiple times
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use DYNAMIC_SECTION or incorporate counter
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Good loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        DYNAMIC_SECTION("Section " << i) {  // Unique name per iteration
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

### 2. **THREAD SAFETY - ASSERTIONS ARE NOT THREAD-SAFE**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([]() {
            REQUIRE(some_calculation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
        });
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Synchronize results, test on main thread
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    std::atomic<int> passed{0};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([&passed]() {
            if (some_calculation() == expected) {
                passed++;
            }
        });
    }
    
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    REQUIRE(passed == 4);  // Test results on main thread
}
```

### 3. **EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION - AVOID BINARY OPERATORS**
❌ **WRONG**: Cannot decompose properly
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0 && b < 10);  // Shows "false" on failure, not individual values
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Split into separate assertions
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0);
REQUIRE(b < 10);  // Each shows individual values on failure
```

### 4. **FLOATING POINT - NEVER USE APPROX**
❌ **WRONG**: Approx is deprecated and asymmetric
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_value == Catch::Approx(expected));  // Deprecated!
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use floating point matchers
```cpp
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));     // 4 ULPs apart
```

### 5. **TEST ORDERING - ALWAYS USE RANDOM ORDER**
✅ **REQUIRED**: For CI/CD and development
```bash
# Essential flags for running tests
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# For test sharding (parallel execution), share random seed
./tests --order rand --shard-index 0 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
```

## Overview of OrcaSlicer's Testing Framework

OrcaSlicer uses **Catch2 v3** (currently v3.11.0, vendored in `tests/catch2/`) as its primary testing framework. The test suite is organized into several modules that mirror the project's architectural components:

> **Note**: Test files include the framework via `#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>` (the v3 single-header convenience include). All v3 features described in this guide are available.

### Test Structure
```
tests/
├── CMakeLists.txt              # Main test configuration
├── catch_main.hpp              # Custom test reporter
├── libslic3r/                  # Core library tests (21 test files)
├── fff_print/                  # FFF printing tests (12 test files)
├── sla_print/                  # SLA printing tests (4 test files)
├── libnest2d/                  # 2D nesting tests
├── slic3rutils/               # Utility tests
├── data/                      # Test data files and meshes
└── catch2/                    # Catch2 framework files
```

### Build Integration
- Tests are built using CMake with `catch_discover_tests()` integration
- Each test module creates a separate executable (e.g., `libslic3r_tests`, `fff_print_tests`)
- Test data directory is available via `TEST_DATA_DIR` preprocessor definition
- Custom verbose console reporter provides detailed test output

## Test Suite Organization

### libslic3r Tests
Core slicing engine tests covering:
- **Geometry operations**: Points, polygons, lines, Voronoi diagrams
- **File formats**: STL, 3MF, AMF parsing and validation
- **Algorithms**: Clipper operations, mesh boolean operations, optimization
- **Configuration**: Print settings validation and parsing
- **Utilities**: String processing, time utilities, data structures

### fff_print Tests
Fused Filament Fabrication specific tests:
- **G-code generation**: Writer functionality, cooling, lift/unlift
- **Slicing algorithms**: Layer generation, infill patterns
- **Print mechanics**: Flow calculations, extrusion, support material
- **Model processing**: Print objects, skirt/brim generation

### sla_print Tests
Stereolithography specific tests:
- **SLA print processing**: Layer curing, support generation
- **Raycast operations**: Light path calculations
- **Test utilities**: SLA-specific helper functions

## Writing New Tests - Best Practices

### File Organization
1. **Naming Convention**: `test_<feature>.cpp` (e.g., `test_geometry.cpp`)
2. **Header Structure**: Include `<catch2/catch_all.hpp>` first, then relevant headers
3. **Namespace Usage**: Use `using namespace Slic3r;` for convenience
4. **File Placement**: Add to appropriate test directory and update CMakeLists.txt

### Test Naming and Structure
```cpp
#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>
#include "libslic3r/Point.hpp"

using namespace Slic3r;

TEST_CASE("Feature description", "[category_tag]") {
    // Test implementation
}
```

### Tagging System
Use descriptive tags for test categorization:
- `[Geometry]` - Geometric operations and calculations
- `[GCodeWriter]` - G-code generation functionality  
- `[Config]` - Configuration and settings tests
- `[FileFormat]` - File I/O operations (STL, 3MF, etc.)
- `[Algorithm]` - Core algorithms and processing
- `[Performance]` - Performance benchmarks (if applicable)

## Catch2 Features Guide

### Basic Assertions
```cpp
// Primary assertions - stop test on failure
REQUIRE(expression);
REQUIRE_FALSE(expression);

// Continuing assertions - continue test after failure  
CHECK(expression);
CHECK_FALSE(expression);

// Non-failing checks - record result but don't fail test
CHECK_NOFAIL(expression);  // Useful for assumptions that might be violated
```

### Exception Testing
```cpp
// Verify no exception is thrown
REQUIRE_NOTHROW(function_call());

// Verify any exception is thrown
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());

// Verify specific exception type
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(function_call(), SpecificException);

// Verify exception message
REQUIRE_THROWS_WITH(function_call(), "Expected error message");

// Verify exception with matchers (for partial matching)
REQUIRE_THROWS_MATCHES(function_call(), SpecificException, 
                       Catch::Matchers::Message("contains this"));
```

### Complex Assertions with Matchers
```cpp
#include <catch2/matchers/catch_matchers.hpp>

// String matchers
using Catch::Matchers::StartsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::EndsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::ContainsSubstring;
using Catch::Matchers::Equals;
using Catch::Matchers::Matches;  // Regex matching

REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, StartsWith("Expected prefix"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, ContainsSubstring("middle part"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, Matches(".*pattern.*"));

// Floating point matchers - ALWAYS use these instead of Approx!
using Catch::Matchers::WithinAbs;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinRel;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinULP;

REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));     // Absolute tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));      // Relative tolerance (1%)
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));         // ULP difference (requires IEEE-754)

// Combining matchers
REQUIRE_THAT(value, WithinRel(expected, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));
```

### Sections for Test Organization
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Complex feature testing", "[Feature]") {
    // Common setup code
    SomeObject obj;
    
    SECTION("First scenario") {
        // Specific test case
        REQUIRE(obj.method1() == expected_value);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second scenario") {
        // Another test case with same setup
        REQUIRE(obj.method2() == other_expected);
    }
}
```

### BDD-Style Tests
Use for complex scenarios and user story testing:

> **Note**: BDD macros are aliases for TEST_CASE and SECTION with prefixed names
```cpp
SCENARIO("User performs complex operation", "[UserStory]") {
    GIVEN("A specific setup condition") {
        GCodeWriter writer;
        // Setup code
        
        WHEN("User performs action") {
            auto result = writer.some_operation();
            
            THEN("Expected outcome occurs") {
                REQUIRE(result.size() > 0);
                
                AND_WHEN("Follow-up action occurs") {
                    auto next_result = writer.next_operation();
                    
                    THEN("Final outcome is correct") {
                        REQUIRE(next_result == expected);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Data Generators for Parameterized Tests
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Function works with various inputs", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto test_value = GENERATE(1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13);
    
    REQUIRE(is_odd(test_value));
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Range-based generators
TEST_CASE("Range testing", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto i = GENERATE(range(1, 10));  // 1 to 9
    REQUIRE(process_value(i) > i);
}

// Using variables in generators (requires GENERATE_COPY or GENERATE_REF)
TEST_CASE("Generator with variables", "[Algorithm]") {
    std::vector<int> values = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    auto test_value = GENERATE_REF(from_range(values));  // Use GENERATE_REF for references
    
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Custom generators
TEST_CASE("Random values", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto random_int = GENERATE(take(100, random(-1000, 1000)));  // 100 random values
    REQUIRE(process_random_value(random_int));
}
```

### Test Fixtures
```cpp
class GeometryFixture {
public:
    Point origin{0, 0};
    Point unit_x{1, 0};
    Point unit_y{0, 1};
    
    mutable double tolerance = EPSILON;  // Use mutable for data that might change
};

// Standard fixture - new instance per test run
TEST_CASE_METHOD(GeometryFixture, "Point operations", "[Geometry]") {
    REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
}

// Persistent fixture - single instance for entire test case (v3.2.0+)
TEST_CASE_PERSISTENT_FIXTURE(GeometryFixture, "Persistent operations", "[Geometry]") {
    static int call_count = 0;
    ++call_count;
    INFO("This fixture persists across sections, call: " << call_count);
    
    SECTION("First section") {
        REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second section") {
        REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_y) == 1.0);
        // call_count will be 2 here with persistent fixture
    }
}

// Template fixtures for type-parameterized tests
template<typename T>
class NumericFixture {
public:
    T zero = T{0};
    T one = T{1};
};

TEMPLATE_TEST_CASE_METHOD(NumericFixture, "Numeric operations", "[Template]", int, float, double) {
    REQUIRE(TestType{} == this->zero);
```

## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)

### Memory Management
Use RAII and smart pointers in tests:
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Resource management", "[Memory]") {
    auto model = std::make_unique<Model>();
    // Automatic cleanup on test completion/failure
    
    REQUIRE(model->objects.empty());
}
```

1. Create test file: `test_new_feature.cpp`

```cmake
    TEST_PREFIX "${_TEST_NAME}: "
    TEST_SUFFIX " (auto)"
    WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}
    EXTRA_ARGS --order rand --warn NoAssertions
```

## Known Issues and Workarounds

### Platform-Specific Issues
```cpp
// MinGW/CygWin slow linking workaround
// Use: -fuse-ld=lld flag to speed up linking significantly

// Visual Studio 2017 raw string literal bug
#define CATCH_CONFIG_DISABLE_STRINGIFICATION
// This disables expression stringification but works around the compiler bug

// QNX/VxWorks C stdlib issues

// NOT: #include <foo.h> and foo_function();
```

### Catch2 v3 Features Available
```cpp
// OrcaSlicer is on Catch2 v3.11.0 - all of these ARE available:

// - Sections can still be re-run if a later section fails (unchanged from v2)
```

#### Project Structure Rules
1. **1:1 correspondence**: One test binary per library/module
2. **Hidden tests**: Use `[.]` or `[!benchmark]` tags for tests that shouldn't run by default
3. **Tag hierarchy**: Use consistent tagging scheme across the project

Kenneth decided (2026-09-28) that prompt changes are evaluated on DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, pinned to hosts that answer the app's developer notes (`tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py` defaults), and on no other model. I had kept running and reporting the app's own gpt-5.4-mini next to it on every change; he asked why I treated the app's model as special, and had me remove the `--app` option and every "also check the app's model" instruction.

**Why:** it doubled cost and numbers to read, made the app's model look like a second judge, and JusPrin will soon support other providers, so today's default model isn't what users will necessarily get.

**How to apply:** judge and report prompt edits with the harness defaults only (paired `--prompt-rev HEAD` run). Use `--model` only when he asks to compare models. The real-app check (`shell_harness --printer-live`) still uses whatever the app is configured with; that's an app check, not a prompt evaluation. See [[fix-without-breaking-other-scenarios]].

content.text:
DeepSeek is now the only model used to judge prompt changes. The change is committed as `24cb890f45`.

**In the test script (`run_prompt_tests.py`):**
- I removed the `--app` option. That was the shortcut to the app's own model, and nothing else in the script ran it.
- Its help text now says prompt changes are judged on DeepSeek V4 Flash, on the fixed set of OpenRouter hosts, and nothing else.
- `--model` still lets you try another model, but only for comparing models, not for judging a prompt change.

**In the README:**
- I removed the instruction to "run it once more with `--app` before a prompt change ships", along with all other `--app` mentions.
- The baseline table now shows DeepSeek's before and after results only: 78 → 79 of 87.
- The case count now says 29.
- I kept the four-model comparison table, because it records why DeepSeek was chosen.

I ran it twice to check: a normal run uses DeepSeek on the fixed hosts, and `--app` is now rejected as an unknown option.

**Left unchanged on purpose:**
- **The live test in the real app** (`--printer-live`) still uses whichever model the app is set up with. It checks that the app works, not the wording of the prompt.
- **Earlier commit messages** still quote app-model numbers. They're history, and changing them would mean rewriting commits.

I also saved the decision to memory, so future sessions stick to DeepSeek alone.
